world-0492a14b61.headline: IDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoff
world-0492a14b61.fulltext:
An Israeli soldier has shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupied West Bank.
Witnesses said a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.
Reached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.
“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”
Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.
“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”
Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.
The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man, apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.
Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.
The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.
On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.
Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.
After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.
It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.
Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.
East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.
On 4 September, two Palestinian teenagers were shot dead in al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.
The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.

beyond-your-beat-b0873ff01d.headline: Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize
beyond-your-beat-b0873ff01d.fulltext:
May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.
Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.
The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as “elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.
Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually, Venice doesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.
In an emotional acceptance speech, El-Toukhy thanked Gyllenhaal for addressing the underrepresentation of female film-makers at the start of the festival. Woman Unknown was the only film in competition to be solely directed by a woman.
“This film has been incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” El-Toukhy said. “And what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known. And especially tonight, I feel like I succeeded in doing just that.”
The runner-up grand jury prize went to the Korean director Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, a simmering tale of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband, which drew rave reviews.
The special jury prize, Venice’s equivalent of a bronze medal, went to Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA, about Israel’s AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza.
The film, which was produced by the Guardian, is based on testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders who are interviewed anonymously at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv. It takes its title from an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.
“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the Israeli politicians and journalists who are now attacking this film and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said when accepting his prize. “So much is being done not to look at reality.”
The day after NAZA’s premiere, the Israeli military “categorically denied” the allegations made in the film.
The Russian director Ilya Khrzhanovsky won the Silver Lion for best director for the visually stunning DAU, a biopic of the Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau, who was pressured into working on the Soviet Union’s nuclear weapons programme.
The inclusion of Khrzhanovsky’s film in the Venice lineup was criticised by the Ukrainian government in the run-up to the festival, over its lead actor Teodor Currentzis’s refusal to condemn the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and for having received funding from a Russian businessman who was later sanctioned by the US and Ukraine.
DAU was filmed in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011, before the start of the conflict. At a press conference on the Lido, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”
John Malkovich took home the Volpi Cup for best actor, for his role as an erratic veteran CIA agent whose cancer diagnosis leads him to question the morality of his profession, in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine.
The 72-year-old US actor was not present in Venice and accepted his award via a video link. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice film festival,” Malkovich said.
Full list of winners

Grand jury prize: Possible Love, directed by Lee Chang-dong
Silver Lion for best director: Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAU
Special jury prize: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor
Best screenplay: Un bon petit soldat (A Good Little Soldier), Stéphane Brizé, Coralie Amédéo, Olivier Gorce
Volpi Cup for best actress: Mathilde Arcel in Woman Unknown
Volpi Cup for best actor: John Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine
Marcello Mastroianni award for best young actor: Malou Khebizi in 15/18 A Place to Heal
Armani Beauty audience award: Eu contez (I Matter), directed by Alina Șerban
Luigi De Laurentiis award for debut film: La maison du vent (House of the Wind), directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu

other-interests-1dd50842d7.headline: SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike
other-interests-1dd50842d7.fulltext:
Dozens of temporary gas turbines in Mississippi powering a huge SpaceXAI data centre in neighbouring Tennessee have caused a major spike in nitrogen oxide air pollution, satellite data suggests. SpaceXAI and local authorities dispute the claim.
SpaceXAI’s Colossus 2 data centre in Tennessee came online in 2025 and is now the largest operational data centre in the US, servicing the firm’s rapidly growing artificial intelligence technology.
However, the site has been embroiled in controversy over its use of temporary gas turbines. Campaigners say these turbines are contributing to hazardous levels of air pollution in the surrounding area, and there are ongoing legal cases over their use, pursued by campaigners and local residents against SpaceXAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech.
Advertisement
Normally, emissions of NOx and other air pollutants from gas power plants are controlled using catalytic converters, but most of the temporary turbines powering the Colossus 2 plant don’t have them fitted.
NOx gases can inflame the airways and exacerbate the symptoms of people already suffering from lung or heart conditions. They also react with other air pollutants to form ozone and particulate matter, both key components of urban smog.
Kevin Gauld at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his colleagues used observations from NASA’s TEMPO satellite – launched in 2023 to monitor air pollution over North America – to assess the impact of the Colossus 2 plant on local air quality.
The satellite observations show a “strong increase” in local NOx concentrations from late 2025 onwards, according to the study by Gauld’s team, which is when SpaceXAI began deploying the temporary turbines to Colossus 2.
The researchers then used the TEMPO satellite to calculate two-week-average NOx source rates from August 2025 to mid-August 2026. They first detected NOx emissions in December 2025, and emissions increased throughout the study period. The number of turbines on the site rose during the study period, from 27 in December 2025 to 69 by August 2026.
The satellite analysis suggests that emissions averaged about 730 kilograms per hour between February and August 2026, peaking at 1180 kg per hour in August 2026. By comparison, the monthly emissions from a nearby gas power plant in Mississippi averaged just 21 kilograms per hour of NOx emissions, the paper reports.
Martyn Chipperfield at the University of Leeds in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the study, says the pollution levels observed by the satellite are significant. “The values they report in the vicinity of the [temporary turbines] are values that we have seen over central London,” he says.
Ronald Cohen at the University of California, Berkeley, says the paper is “solid” science. “It’s very clear that there’s a huge number of uncontrolled generators on this site, generators without emissions controls on them,” he says. “There’s a lot of electricity being created, and they are putting a lot of NO2 [the most commonly regulated NOx gas] into the atmosphere.”
Peter Zoogman at Minerva University, California, who worked on the development of the TEMPO satellite, says the NOx emissions, as calculated in the paper, would mean each turbine was producing roughly the same level of emissions each year as 50,000 cars. He called for further work to quantify the health impacts of the emissions, including measuring any change in the local levels of ozone pollution since the opening of the site.
In July 2026, SpaceXAI promised to remove all 69 temporary turbines by July 2027 and replace them with 41 permanent gas turbines. The company was granted permission to construct the permanent gas turbines in March 2026 by the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ). SpaceXAI also promised that all of the mobile turbines it uses – which it is starting to manufacture in-house – will be fitted with pollution-control technology.
“Making sure these converters are fitted to these power generation systems is very important,” says Zoogman. “It does make a very large difference.”
However, the satellite study concludes that the current average emissions rate from the temporary turbines is about 16 times higher than it is expected to be once the permanent turbines are installed.
Responding to queries from New Scientist, SpaceXAI sent a court submission from a third-party air-quality expert, which claims local air-quality monitoring stations haven’t observed notable increases in pollution concentrations since the mobile generators began operating. It said the emissions from the site fall within the relevant regulatory requirements.
A statement from MDEQ in response to questions from New Scientist said: “MDEQ does not comment on third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation. MDEQ recognizes the public interest in this facility and remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations.”
The satellite analysis comes as concern grows over the rapid rollout of new gas power to run the massive new data centres that underpin the booming AI sector. US gas-fired power under development jumped by 50 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor, an independent non-profit.
Meanwhile, almost half of the proposals for powering data centres with gas involve using gas turbines and engines. These are less efficient and more polluting than combined cycle plants – which reuse waste heat from one turbine to power another – but are quicker to deploy. Experts warn this new gas build-out will lock in decades of additional carbon emissions and worsen air quality. Many data centres also rely on diesel generators for back-up power, which emit high levels of NOx and other pollutants.
Data centres may also need close monitoring to check that the new dedicated power plants supporting the facilities are meeting regulatory requirements. “That’s why having this public attention on it is really valuable,” says Zoogman. “I think it’s important to have this technology to do the monitoring and the assessment and figure out where the pollution is coming from.”
Rapid advances in satellite technology mean they are increasingly being used to spot unreported emissions across a whole range of sectors, including oil and gas infrastructure, landfills and manufacturing facilities.

other-interests-d159a0668e.headline: How burnt coconut helped discover new to science endemic species in Sri Lanka
other-interests-d159a0668e.fulltext:
- Scientists have formally described Mus dumbara, a new species of spiny mouse from Sri Lanka’s Dumbara or Knuckles Mountain Range after years of waiting.
- Collected for the first time in 2004, it took more than two decades of morphological and genetic analysis to establish it as a distinct species from the other spiny mouse species found in Sri Lanka.
- Subsequent efforts to find fresh specimens of the elusive mouse proved unsuccessful, despite around 1,900 trap nights in the area, leaving scientists with limited information about its current population and distribution.
- Found only from a small area of the Knuckles Range so far, the discovery highlights the island’s overlooked biodiversity of small mammals and the need for further surveys to understand the species’ ecology and conservation needs.
COLOMBO — As dusk settled over the paddy fields at Puwakpitiya, a village on the northern edge of Knuckles Mountain Range locally known as Dumbara mountains in Central Sri Lanka, researchers began laying traps along the uneasy boundary between farmland and forest.
They were targeting small terrestrial mammals moving through the landscape. On the ground, drift fences were created to lead animals to pitfall traps, while box style Sherman live traps were baited with feed. But the usual rodent lure — peanut butter — failed to attract the mice in Sri Lanka, so the researchers instead turned to something more familiar to the local mice — pieces of burnt coconut.
On March 11, 2004, one of the pitfall traps caught a small mouse that looked different. Six days later, a second specimen was caught in a baited trap. Both were females, not larger than a child’s palm, with fulvous-gray pelage broken by spiny guard hairs and a slender, naked tail longer than the head and body. Externally, the animal resembled Mayor’s mouse (Mus mayori), a species endemic to Sri Lanka’s highlands, but differed in tail length and head shape, offering initial clues about a new species.
The two mice remained a scientific mystery for more than two decades, but careful genetic and morphological evidence finally confirmed what researchers had suspected all along, and they soon introduced a species new to science. It’s been named Mus dumbara, commonly known as the Dumbara valley’s spiny mouse, a name that links the rodent to its locality.
Sri Lanka is home to 16 species of rats and mice with six of them endemic. The new discovery adds another endemic mammal to Sri Lanka’s list.
An elusive new rodent
“The Dumbara spiny mouse looks elusive,” said study lead author Suyama Boyagoda, current head of the department of zoology and chairperson of the board of study in zoological sciences at the Postgraduate Institute of Science (PGIS), University of Peradeniya. At the time of discovering the spiny mouse, Boyagoda was researching shrews in Sri Lanka for her Ph.D.
“In 2014 and 2015, I returned to the same locality and setup a number of traps, but despite the investment of 1,900 trap nights employing the same trapping methods, we failed to find a mouse similar to the first specimen,” Boyagoda told Mongabay.
The new species belongs to the subgenus Pyromys and can be distinguished from its closest Sri Lankan relatives, Mus fernandoni and Mus mayori, by a combination of physical characteristics, she said. Its tail is distinctly longer than its head-and-body length. Its hind feet have pinkish-white toes, while the remaining dorsal surface is covered by a mixture of fulvous-brown, gray and white hairs.
The skull provided additional clues as M. dumbara has a moderately prominent ridge above the eye socket, known as a supraorbital ridge. The strongest evidence came from the DNA showing more than 11.7% genetic divergence between M. dumbara and the other two species, Boyagoda noted.
Sri Lanka and India’s Western Ghats together form one of the world’s most recognized biodiversity hotspots. Although temporary land connections across the Palk Strait linked the island with southern India during Pleistocene glacial periods, Sri Lanka’s wildlife has remained isolated for long enough to evolve along a distinct path.
This is particularly evident in the island’s wet-zone and montane forests, where exceptional levels of endemism have developed, said Madhava Meegaskumbura, a Sri Lankan evolutionary biologist and researcher at Guangxi University in China.
Meegaskumbura, a co-author of the new study, was among the initial research team and, in fact, collected the first specimen of this elusive mouse along with Sri Lankan biologist Mohammed Bahir.
Less researched small mammals
“In recent decades, scientists have described numerous new species of frogs, lizards and freshwater crabs. Mammals, however, have produced comparatively few such discoveries, partly because they tend to be larger and more readily detected. The discovery of Mus dumbara adds another species to this relatively short list of recently recognized Sri Lankan mammals,” Meegaskumbura said.
So far, M. dumbara has been recorded from just one valley in the Knuckles Range, leaving considerable uncertainty about its true distribution and population size. The species may occur in other forest fragments that have not been surveyed, or survive at very low densities, or may have experienced a decline since the first specimens were collected, Meegaskumbura noted.
Even though Knuckles Range is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with formal protection, less conspicuous mammals can easily be overlooked in conservation planning. Habitats along the forest margins remain particularly vulnerable to road construction, land clearance, encroachment and the expansion of plantations.
For a species apparently restricted to a limited elevational range, these pressures could be compounded by climate change, which may reduce the availability of suitable habitat and potential refuges, Boyagoda added. Given the limited information currently available, Meegaskumbura added that M. dumbara should be treated cautiously as a species potentially at risk of extinction until further surveys establish its actual distribution and population status.
“Very little research has been carried out on Sri Lanka’s small mammals, and several important gaps remain, where we need extensive island-wide surveys to understand their distributions and habitat associations and to determine whether undescribed or overlooked species like Mus dumbara remain,” said Sampath Goonatilake, a researcher with IUCN Sri Lanka who studies small mammals. “One of the biggest needs is a comprehensive taxonomic revision, using both classical taxonomy and modern phylogenetic approaches, to clarify the identity, classification and evolutionary relationships of the species we currently recognize.”
“The lack of research is partly because studying small mammals is demanding and expensive as researchers may have to spend weeks or even months in forest habitats to obtain enough samples, creating substantial logistical and fieldwork costs, Goonatilake told Mongabay.
There are also relatively few up-to-date identification guides for Sri Lanka’s small mammals, which makes accurate field identification more difficult. At the same time, these animals tend to attract less attention from researchers and students than larger or more charismatic mammals. Addressing these gaps will require sustained funding, as a comprehensive taxonomic and island-wide research program could cost several million rupees, so collaboration among Sri Lankan universities, government agencies, museums and international research institutions, supported by external research grants and international funding, will be essentia.

opportunities-f78b1b8970.headline: PanIIT Andhra Pradesh Summit to be held in Vijayawada on October 3
opportunities-f78b1b8970.fulltext:
The PanIIT Andhra Pradesh Summit 2026, aimed at fostering a DeepTech and technology-driven ecosystem in the State, will be held in Vijayawada on October 3.
Organised by PanIIT Alumni India, the summit will be held at the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Convention Centre under the theme “Andhra’s DeepTech Decade: Anchored by PanIIT – Swarnandhra to Viksit Bharat 2047”. Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu will be the chief guest, while Education, IT and Electronics Minister Nara Lokesh will participate.
The summit will bring together IIT directors and faculty, government officials, industry leaders, investors, entrepreneurs and technology experts to explore opportunities in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, data centres, quantum technologies, defence and aerospace, green energy, healthcare, AgriTech and AI-enabled governance.
The organisers said the summit would seek to strengthen collaboration among the government, IITs, industry, investors and startups, with a focus on research, innovation, investment and skill development.
Proposals to be discussed include setting up a PanIIT Amaravati Council, creating DeepTech investment mechanisms and establishing a Global IIT Mentor Network to connect entrepreneurs and young talent in Andhra Pradesh with the wider IIT alumni and technology ecosystem.
PanIIT officials said the summit would focus on leveraging the State’s talent, infrastructure and strategic advantages to attract investment and create opportunities in innovation and employment.

opportunities-9a5d2697e0.fulltext:
Jaipur Literature Festival to mark 20 years with landmark 2027 edition
The festival will mark its 20th edition from January 14-18, 2027, celebrating two decades of literary exchange, multilingual storytelling and global dialogue.
Jaipur, Sept 10: The Jaipur Literature Festival (JLF) will mark its 20th edition in January 2027, celebrating two decades of bringing writers, thinkers, artists and readers together for literary exchange, cultural dialogue and conversations across languages and disciplines.
The landmark edition of the festival, supported by the Government of Rajasthan, will be held in Jaipur from January 14 to 18, 2027, under the theme “20 Years of Ideas. Stories. Conversations.”
Since its inception in 2008, JLF has hosted more than 8,000 writers, speakers and artists and welcomed over five million visitors on the ground. Its digital platforms, broadcast partnerships and media networks have reached an estimated audience of more than one billion, according to the festival organisers.
What began as a gathering of writers and readers in Jaipur has grown into an international literary platform, with more than 15 editions held across countries including the US, UK, Canada, Spain, Australia, the Middle East, the Maldives and Ireland.
The festival has also sought to broaden access to literature by bringing literary discussions into wider public conversations. Its programming spans literature, history, politics, science, philosophy, economics, arts, gender, health, migration and the environment.
A key focus of the 20th edition will be India's linguistic diversity. Over the years, the festival has featured writers and literary traditions in multiple Indian and international languages and promoted translation and cross-linguistic exchange.
As part of the anniversary celebrations, the festival's announcement has been released simultaneously in all 22 official languages of India, highlighting its emphasis on multilingual storytelling.
Namita Gokhale, Festival Co-Director, Jaipur Literature Festival, said the festival's 20th year was an opportunity to recognise India's linguistic heritage.
“The soul of India lies in her literary heritage and linguistic diversity. It is only appropriate that we celebrate our milestone 20th year with a tribute to her many languages through our Bhasha Swarmala series,” Gokhale said.
Sanjoy K. Roy, Managing Director of Teamwork Arts and Producer of JLF, said the festival's journey had been sustained by writers, audiences and a commitment to dialogue across cultures and perspectives.
“For twenty years, the Jaipur Literature Festival has been built on a simple belief that books and ideas have the power to bring people together. As we enter our twentieth edition, we celebrate that journey while looking ahead to the many conversations still to come,” Roy said.
Preeta Singh, President, Teamwork Arts, said the festival had grown into a global literary and cultural platform while remaining rooted in books, ideas and dialogue.
The festival's relationship with the Government of Rajasthan has continued since its inception and has been described by the organisers as integral to its growth. The partnership has also helped position Jaipur and Rajasthan within the global literary and cultural landscape.
As it enters its third decade, JLF said it would continue to focus on making literature and ideas accessible to audiences across generations, languages and geographies, while creating spaces for diverse voices and perspectives.
The festival was founded in 2006 and its first edition was held in 2008, according to the organisers.
